extracted.intended_audience: medical, dental, and public health students learning practical bacteriology
extracted.subtask_description: Practical laboratory protocols and evaluative principles for studying pathogenic bacteria, preparing museum specimens, and performing bacteriological analyses (quantitative and qualitative) of samples such as water. Includes sampling, transport, culture, identification, controls, and specimen preservation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autopsy card / Post Mortem documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Autopsy card fields and notes for recording post-mortem examinations (Laboratory No., Date, Animal, Weight, time died/killed, time autopsy made). Sections for Notes on Post Mortem Examinations: General; A. Seat of Inoculation; B. Thoracic Cavity; C. Abdominal Cavity; D. Cranial Cavity. Separate columns/headings for Bacteriological Examination, Histological Examination, Organs Preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the card to indicate positions of chief lesions; include bacteriological and histological findings and list organs preserved. The card front/back illustrations (Fig. 200/201) are models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of isolated organisms with clinical symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Results of action of isolated organisms should be correlated with symptoms observed during life and summarised under 'Tissue changes' and 'Symptoms'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tissue changes: (1) Local (position: primary lesion or secondary foci; character: vascular changes and tissue reactions OR degeneration and necrosis) — acute or chronic. (2) General (toxin absorption): effects in special tissues or general effects such as malnutrition. Symptoms: (a) associated with known tissue changes; (b) without known tissue changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent Preparations -- Museum Specimens (tissues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to preserve naked-eye appearances of morbid tissues as museum specimens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: remove tissue promptly avoiding distortion; place in wide-mouthed stoppered jar on cotton-wool pad in intended position; cover with Kaiserling fixing solution and fix 48 hours–7 days (depending on size); make sections as necessary; transfer to methylated spirit (95%) 30–60 minutes; then fresh spirit until natural colours return (3–6 hours average); dry cut surfaces and transfer to mounting solution. Kaiserling modified solution composition: potassium acetate 30g, potassium nitrate 15g, dissolved in 1000 c.c. distilled water, then add 150 c.c. formalin; filter. Mounting solutions: Jore's (glycerine 500 c.c., distilled water 750 c.c., formalin 2 c.c.) or Frost's (potassium acetate 160g, sodium fluoride 80g, chloral hydrate 80g, cane sugar 3500g, saturated thymol water 8000 c.c.). After ~24 hours in mounting solution or when tissue sinks, transfer to museum jar, fill with fresh mounting solution and seal; alternative: fill with liquefied gelatine +1% formalin and allow to set. Sealing: warm cover plate, smear hot cement (gutta percha 4 parts + asphaltum 5 parts melted), invert plate, press with weight until set, trim, burr joint with hot metal, finish with Japan black paint around joint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent Preparations -- Tube cultivations (museum specimens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preservation of tube cultures as long-term museum specimens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a large glass jar with ground flange and a plate glass lid; smear resin ointment on flange; layer cotton-wool saturated with formalin at jar bottom; place culture tubes mouth upward inside jar (remove condensation before placing); adjust ground glass disc over mouth pressing into ointment; leave for one week; dry tubes and seal open mouths in blowpipe flame, label. For museum planting use Bulloch's tubes (longer with constriction ~2 cm below mouth) to ease sealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study method for pathogenic bacteria — pure cultivations and group study
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should work from pure cultivations to study life-history of pathogenic bacteria and record observations to be corrected/amplified by demonstrator; study bacteria in groups to learn resemblances and differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify textbook descriptions by personal observation. Study allied or resembling organisms in parallel ('groups') so repetition builds familiarity with cultural and morphological characters. The author’s grouping scheme is recommended for elementary classes; details vary with demonstrator and student requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping taxonomy for practical study of pathogenic bacteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical grouping of pathogenic bacteria into named groups (e.g., Organisms of Suppuration / pyogenic bacteria; Pneumonia group; Diphtheroid group; Coli-typhoid group; Escherich group; Gaertner group; Eberth group; Spirillum group; Anthrax group; Acid fast group; Plague group; Influenzae group; Streptothrix group; Tetanus group; Enteritidis sporogenes group; Miscellaneous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these groups to structure laboratory study and comparisons; some bacteria appear in more than one group which aids learning by repetition. The page lists organisms under each group for targeted study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical protocol for studying pyogenic cocci (media, temperatures, observations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific culture and microscopic examination regime to contrast staphylococci and related micrococci.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare subcultivations on bouillon, agar streak, blood serum, litmus milk and incubate at 37°C; on agar streak, gelatine stab, potato incubate at 20°C. Compare naked-eye culture appearances daily. Make hanging-drop preparations after 24 hours; prepare cover-slip films, stain for flagella by modified Pitfield's method; note locomotive activity (e.g., M. agilis shows flagella). Make microscopic preparations after 24h, 48h, 3 days; stain with carbolic methylene-blue, carbolic fuchsin, and Gram's method to note Gram-negative/dead cocci in 3-day growth. Stain tissue sections (e.g., kidney abscess) by Gram and counterstain with cosin; stain pus films similarly. Experimental virulence test: inoculate mouse subcutaneously with defined inoculum of S. aureus and observe life course and post-mortem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bacteriological analyses — quantitative vs qualitative
rubrics_metrics.description: Each bacteriological analysis generally includes: (1) Quantitative (enumeration of total bacteria present), and (2) Qualitative (identification of pathogenic bacteria and their numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative is of minor importance (approximate total numbers). Qualitative is more important and both qualitative and quantitative aspects are used to identify pathogenic bacteria while indicating their numerical frequency. Methods given are adaptable to various sample types (water, sewage, food, filters, germicides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls in experimental bacteriology
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity for adequate controls in all experimental work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every batch of plates should include at least one 'sterile' medium control; plate/tube cultures should be made from diluting fluids; every inoculated tube of carbohydrate medium should incubate alongside a similar uninoculated tube. Controls are essential for validating sterility and procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature selection for water bacteriology
rubrics_metrics.description: Incubate cultivations at both 20°C and 37°C to demonstrate different bacterial classes present in water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 20°C favors varieties with normal habitat in water (environmental bacteria) and development of moulds/yeasts/torulae (best plated in wort gelatine). 37°C demonstrates varieties derived from/excremental for animal bodies (pathogenic) which grow well at body temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection of water samples — vessels and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Sterilized small glass bottles (60 c.c., narrow necks, glass stoppers) are most suitable; collection procedures differ for taps/pipes, streams, lakes/reservoirs, and deep samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From tap/pipe: run water for a few minutes, fill ~3/4, replace stopper but do not seal. From stream: attach wire handle to bottle, plunge mouth downward, reverse to fill, pour out a few c.c., replace stopper and tie. For varying depths use Esmarch's apparatus (weighted cage, remote-opening bottle). Alternatives: construct deep-sampling bottle with rubber-cork and two glass tubes connected by tubing and weighted to open on jerk; sterilise in autoclave; methods prevent contamination. Illustrations (Figs. 203–205) show recommended devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport of water samples — prevent multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: If examination cannot commence immediately, prevent bacterial multiplication during transit by transporting samples in an ice-box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a double-walled metal ice-box with central chamber for bottles, pack space between walls with pounded ice, wrap bottles in cotton-wool, secure lid; place box in felt-lined wooden case. Bacteria survive but do not multiply at near-ice temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative plating method and dilution scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure for adding measured quantities of water sample to liquefied nutrient media, pouring plate cultivations, incubating and counting colonies to estimate organisms per cubic centimetre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare agar and gelatine tubes melted and kept at 42°C. Using sterile 1 c.c. pipettes add 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, and 1.0 c.c. to specific agar tubes numbered 1–6; pour plates and incubate at 37°C. Prepare a 1:100 dilution by adding 0.1 c.c. sample to 9.9 c.c. sterile water for gelatine series and inoculate gelatine tubes similarly to give plate volumes 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.005, 0.003, 0.002 c.c.; incubate gelatine and wort gelatine plates at 20°C. Include uninoculated controls for agar and gelatine. Observe and count colonies at 48 hours and continue observations up to 7 days; calculate organisms per c.c. from average of gelatine plates at latest possible date (watch for liquefying bacteria). Volumes chosen to give workable results across varying bacterial loads; series of plates serve as mutual controls (e.g., plate 2 + 3 ≈ plate 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of counting colonies (Jeffery's and Pakes' discs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of printed counting discs to facilitate accurate colony enumeration and guidance on how much of a plate to count depending on colony density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place plate over counting disc (centre so periphery aligns with concentric circles). Remove cover and use hand lens to count colonies in each sector. If colonies <500, count entire plate. If >500, count half or quarter of the plate or selected sectors and estimate total from those counts. Pakes' disc suits plates with fewer colonies; Jeffery's disc suits denser plates. Note: plates must be carefully leveled and medium of equal thickness—unequal thickness invalidates averaging from small areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales for plate volume selection and inter-plate control
rubrics_metrics.description: The chosen quantities of water added to media are selected to yield workable results across widely differing samples and to provide internal checks between plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agar plates with 0.1 c.c. and gelatine plates with 0.02 c.c. suit samples with large bacterial numbers; agar plate 4 and gelatine plate 1 are reliable when organisms are few. Counts from plates are expected to be proportionally related (e.g., second and third gelatine plates together ≈ first).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative examination focus and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine qualitative examination of water typically searches for B. coli and its near allies, and streptococci as 'microbes of indication' (evidence of pollution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: B. enteritidis sporogenes is less routinely sought because it is relatively scarce and requires more water. In epidemics, new supplies, or unknown waters extend search to other coli-typhoid members and occasionally Vibrio cholerae, B. anthracis, or B. tetani. Pathogenic/excremental bacteria are usually few in number and require enrichment or concentration methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrichment vs Concentration strategies for low-density pathogens
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches when pathogenic/excremental bacteria are present in low numbers: (A) Enrichment — inhibit harmless saprophytes while encouraging parasitic bacteria; (B) Concentration — concentrate all bacteria in a small bulk (e.g., by filtration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enrichment adjusts media, incubation temperature and atmosphere to favor pathogenic organisms (example protocol follows). Concentration is commonly done by filtration through a porcelain candle and emulsifying retained residue into small sterile bouillon volume for further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrichment method protocol for intestinal-origin bacteria (bile salt broth, anaerobic 42°C)
rubrics_metrics.description: A staged protocol using bile salt broth and anaerobic incubation at 42°C to favor intestinal bacteria and suppress ordinary water bacteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary apparatus: incubator at 42°C, sterile pipettes (1 c.c., 10 c.c., 25 c.c.), tubes of bile salt broth and double-strength bile salt broth, litmus milk tubes, sterile flasks, Buchner's tubes, etc. Procedure: number bile salt tubes 1–5 and duplicates 1a–5a; add 0.1, 1, 2, 5, and 10 c.c. water sample respectively to tubes 1–5 and same to duplicates; set up in Buchner's tubes and incubate anaerobically at 42°C. Also inoculate double-strength bile salt broth flasks with 25 c.c. and 50 c.c. sample and incubate aerobically at 42°C. After 24h note visible growth, litmus colour change, gas formation; continue to 48h for tubes with no growth. Remove tubes showing growth for hanging-drop microscopy (note chains of cocci), then prepare surface plates on nutrose agar from tubes showing growth and incubate aerobically at 37°C. Bile salt medium, anaerobiosis and 42°C select for intestinal bacteria while inhibiting ordinary water bacteria; proceed to subcultures, identification (microscopy, biochemical media), and use of agglutinating sera as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification follow-up for coliform/typhiform colonies after enrichment
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure once coliform or typhiform colonies are obtained from enrichment agar plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick colonies and make streak/smear subcultivations on nutrient agar, incubate aerobically 24h at 37°C. Examine macroscopically and microscopically; if impure replate and pick colonies until pure. When pure, emulsify entire surface growth in 5 c.c. sterile normal saline or sterile broth for further identification tests.
